strengths: The paper identifies a useful limitation of curricula that always increase agent counts: additional agents can make cooperative tasks easier. Pursuit provides a concrete, intuitive motivation for learning the direction of the curriculum.

Combining self-paced reinforcement learning with shared-policy IPPO is technically sensible. Jointly adapting agent count and environmental context provides a practical way to avoid prescribing a task ordering.

Figure 3 reports promising improvements in target-task learning speed and mean return, with five-run variability, separate agent-count and grid-size ablations, and comparisons against increasing and decreasing curricula, EPC, and VACL variants.

Reporting limited benefits on Simple-Spread and Simple-Push usefully qualifies the method's applicability. The distinction between summed and averaged rewards also raises an important issue for curricula spanning different population sizes.
weaknesses: The central interpretation of curricula as estimates of task difficulty is insufficiently supported. Section 4.3 defines difficulty through improvement in one policy update, whereas Equation 3 optimizes current expected return through context reweighting. High return need not imply rapid learning or useful transfer to the target task. Direct measurements of learning progress and transfer are needed to establish this interpretation.

The Sum-versus-Average explanation overreaches. For fixed agent count N, averaging simply multiplies the summed reward by 1/N and does not itself introduce competition into a shared-reward task. Across contexts, it changes their relative valuation by the curriculum optimizer. The experiments do not distinguish this scaling effect from changes in coordination difficulty. Moreover, Figure 5 lacks the agent-count-only ablation needed to directly support the claimed reduction in the usefulness of that curriculum variable.

The supported contribution remains narrow relative to the claims. The optimization substantially follows existing SPRL, so the empirical insights carry much of the novelty. Clear performance benefits are concentrated in one Pursuit target configuration; both particle-world tasks converge similarly to the baselines, and the proposed explanations involving collisions and task continuity are not tested through controlled interventions. A fixed randomized-context baseline would also help establish the benefit of adaptive scheduling itself.

Training-budget and baseline fairness are insufficiently documented. The plots label the horizontal axis only as 'Step,' without explaining whether it counts joint environment steps or individual agent transitions. Because shared-policy IPPO collects data from every agent, varying population size can change the available training data and computation. EPC/VACL implementation changes and tuning are also underdescribed. Consequently, the curves do not establish an advantage under clearly matched data or compute budgets.

Important reproduction details are missing despite the appendix tables: the performance threshold V_LB is not clearly reported, the construction of the context-dependent global value estimate from IPPO's local critics is unspecified, and network widths, evaluation episode counts, and bounded-Gaussian discretization details are absent. Threshold sensitivity is particularly relevant because it determines when the curriculum moves toward the target. The introduction's claim of guaranteed comparable convergence also exceeds the evidence provided.
